title: Setting the Stage and the Cold War
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: In March 1946, Winston Churchill declared that 'an iron curtain has descended across the Continent,' from the Baltic to the Adriatic. Behind that line, Soviet-backed communist governments took control of Eastern Europe, and the wartime alliance hardened into suspicion and hostility.

The Cold War was the global rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union from roughly 1945 to 1991. It was called 'cold' because the two superpowers never fought each other directly in open war, a restraint reinforced by their possession of nuclear weapons.

World War II shattered the old European great powers and left two superpowers: the United States and the Soviet Union. Superpowers were states of overwhelming military, economic, and political power with global reach, operating on a different scale from ordinary nations.

The United States championed capitalism and liberal democracy: private property, free markets, multiple political parties, and individual freedoms. It viewed Soviet communism as an aggressive, expansionist tyranny bent on spreading worldwide revolution.

The Soviet Union championed communism: a one-party state, government ownership and central planning of the economy, and the Marxist promise of a classless society, though in practice it was a repressive dictatorship. It viewed American capitalism as an exploitative, imperialist system.

Mutual mistrust drove the Cold War. The Soviets, invaded from the west twice in thirty years, sought to control Eastern Europe as a buffer; the Western Allies saw Stalin's installation of communist regimes as aggression. Each side's defensive moves looked like aggression to the other — a 'security dilemma.'

Containment, articulated by diplomat George Kennan, was the U.S. strategy of firmly resisting the spread of communism wherever it threatened, rather than invading the USSR, in the belief that a contained Soviet system would eventually weaken and collapse from within.

The Truman Doctrine (1947) pledged American support to free peoples resisting communist takeover, beginning with aid to Greece and Turkey. It was an early concrete expression of the containment strategy.

The Marshall Plan (1948) poured billions of dollars into rebuilding war-shattered Western Europe, on the reasoning that prosperous, stable democracies would resist communism's appeal. It was economic aid used as a weapon of containment; the Soviets refused to let Eastern Europe participate.

NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, was the military alliance formed by the United States and Western European nations in 1949 to defend against the Soviet threat, embodying the Western bloc of the Cold War.

The Warsaw Pact (1955) was the Soviet-led military alliance of Eastern European communist states, formed in response to NATO. It embodied the Eastern bloc and bound its members to Soviet military control.

Germany and its capital Berlin were divided into Western and Soviet zones after WWII, leaving West Berlin as an island of capitalist democracy deep inside communist East Germany. Berlin became the Cold War's most dramatic flashpoint.

In 1948–49 Stalin blockaded West Berlin, cutting off all land access to force the Western powers out. The U.S. and Britain responded with the Berlin Airlift, supplying two million West Berliners entirely by air for nearly a year until Stalin lifted the blockade.
In 1961 the East Germans built the Berlin Wall to stop their citizens from fleeing to the West. It became a concrete symbol of the Iron Curtain and stood for nearly three decades until 1989.

Because direct war was too dangerous, the superpowers waged the Cold War through an arms race, a space race, propaganda, espionage, economic competition, and above all proxy conflicts and contests for influence in other countries across the globe.

Both superpowers soon possessed nuclear weapons capable of destroying each other and much of the world. This nuclear shadow is a key reason they avoided direct war and instead competed indirectly, pulling back from the brink in crises.

Europe split into two hostile blocs: the Western bloc (capitalism, liberal democracy, NATO, the Marshall Plan) led by the United States, and the Eastern bloc (communism, state planning, the Warsaw Pact) controlled by the Soviet Union.

The Berlin Airlift established a recurring Cold War pattern: both sides pushed and probed for advantage but pulled back from direct military clash, competing instead through economic power, propaganda, and proxies because the cost of a 'hot' war between nuclear powers was unthinkable.

Analyzing the origins of the Cold War as continuity and change: before 1945 the U.S. and USSR were wartime allies in a multipolar Europe; afterward the alliance collapsed into a bipolar order of two armed blocs and a nuclear arms race, while great-power rivalry and capitalism-vs-communism conflict (since 1917) continued.

The Cold War was the master framework organizing global politics, economics, and culture from 1945 to 1991. Wars, revolutions, coups, the space race, and the arms race were all understood through the lens of the superpower struggle.

The Cold War and decolonization were inseparable: as Europe's empires crumbled after WWII, dozens of new nations were born into a world divided into two armed camps, each desperate to win them over, and their conflicts frequently became proxy battlegrounds of the Cold War.
